meta.title: Who really said "Comedy Is Tragedy Plus Time"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Popularly credited to Carol Burnett, who said she got it from her mother. The earliest known version is Steve Allen's, in Cosmopolitan, February 1957.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Comedy Is Tragedy Plus Time'?
meta.ogDescription: Carol Burnett credited her mother. The earliest known version is Steve Allen's 1957 formula: tragedy plus time equals comedy.

answer.label: Not Carol Burnett — earliest known: Steve Allen
answer.sourceLine: The earliest version Quote Investigator found is Steve Allen’s “Tragedy plus time equals comedy,” printed in his Cosmopolitan column in February 1957. Carol Burnett did popularize the line, and from 1972 on she credited it to her mother (TV Guide, 1972; her 1986 memoir One More Time). QI notes the saying may have been going around before Allen printed it.

source.heading: The earliest documented version
source.excerpt: Man jokes about the things that depress him, but he usually waits till a certain amount of time has passed. It must have been a tragedy when Judge Crater disappeared, but everybody jokes about it now. I guess you can make a mathematical formula out of it. Tragedy plus time equals comedy.
trail: February 1957: Steve Allen writes in Cosmopolitan that “Tragedy plus time equals comedy.” This is the earliest evidence Quote Investigator ↗ found.
1958: Allen repeats it on television and in a UPI interview (QI ↗), now adding “plus the will to be amused.” Barry Popik’s entry ↗ also records the July 1958 Bakersfield Californian printing.
November 1962: Bob Newhart says “They say that comedy is tragedy plus time,” signaling that it was already a saying (Popik ↗).

1963–1986: Carol Burnett offers “Comedy is tragedy mellowed by time” (1963). In TV Guide (1972) she credits “comedy is tragedy plus time” to her mother, and in her memoir One More Time (1986) she gives her mother’s saying as “Most comedy is tragedy plus time” (QI ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is Steve Allen’s wording as Quote Investigator transcribes it from scans of the column. Judge Joseph Crater disappeared in New York in 1930. The phrasing “comedy is tragedy plus time” is a later reshuffle of the same formula.

source.rightsNote: The earliest known wording appears in Steve Allen’s February 1957 Cosmopolitan column. That is a post-1931 work by a named author, so it is treated here as in copyright. Burnett’s variant in her 1986 memoir One More Time is also in copyright. The short adage itself circulates freely as a common saying.

author.name: Steve Allen
author.heading: About the earliest known source
author.bio: Steve Allen co-created The Tonight Show and was its first host. He also hosted The Steve Allen Show and the PBS series Meeting of Minds, and wrote songs and many books. His February 1957 Cosmopolitan column has the earliest documented form of the formula, “Tragedy plus time equals comedy,” which he kept repeating for decades.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: Few comedy maxims have more claimed parents. Every name below really used the formula, but none of them is its documented originator.

items.why: She used the line for decades, but she credited it to someone else. Her 1963 version was “Comedy is tragedy mellowed by time.” In 1972 she told TV Guide that her mother “said comedy is tragedy plus time,” and her 1986 memoir repeats that credit (Quote Investigator ↗). Fred Shapiro of Yale noted that the saying is “usually attributed to Carol Burnett or Woody Allen” and called both attributions “probably apocryphal” (ADS-L, 2011 ↗).

In Allen’s 1989 film Crimes and Misdemeanors, the line belongs to Lester, a character played by Alan Alda. Allen does not say it in his own voice. The film came more than three decades after Steve Allen’s 1957 column (QI ↗).
The Essential Lenny Bruce (1967), published after his death, has him say “satire is tragedy plus time.” That is a later adaptation with “satire” in place of “comedy” (QI ↗).
In 2012, soon after a cancer diagnosis, she used the equation in a celebrated stand-up set: “I am just at tragedy right now.” She was quoting a well-known formula, not coining one (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Steve Allen’s February 1957 Cosmopolitan column is the earliest documented version: “Tragedy plus time equals comedy.” Quote Investigator adds that because Burnett credited her mother, who died in 1958, the saying may have circulated earlier, or her mother may have picked it up from Allen’s column (QI ↗).

context.heading: Why the formula stuck
lead: Allen’s original point was practical. Most comic material is tragic at root (drunkenness, money trouble, accidents), and audiences laugh at disasters once enough time has passed. His example was the 1930 disappearance of Judge Joseph Crater, a mystery that had become a standing joke by the 1950s.

The equation’s neatness made it travel. Comedians kept rephrasing it: Allen added “the will to be amused,” Burnett said “mellowed by time,” and Lenny Bruce swapped in “satire.” Along the way it attached itself to whichever famous comic was saying it most recently.
detailsBody: In an 1889 letter, Thomas Hardy wrote that “All comedy, is tragedy, if you only look deep enough into it.” QI lists this as a related thought, not as the source of the time formula (QI ↗).
